title: Delivering the Storefront: Themes, Headless, Rendering and Performance
basis: Reconstructed from the published chapter (posts/32-storefront-architecture/index.md) and its former spec.md, whose Non-goals, Modalities, Open questions, Decision log, Sources and Changelog are carried over. One spec paragraph per unit of the chapter, plus the units the contract asks for that the published chapter did not have: a roadmap p05, a lead p26 for the requirements table, a lead p53 for the failure table, a synthesis p54 that answers the opening, and a hand-off p59 rewritten as the contrast the next chapter declares; see decision_log.

know: What a storefront owns (templates, layout, brand, browser scripts) and what it renders from other systems; the three rendering models (a theme rendered by the platform, headless on the vendor's runtime, headless anywhere), with checkout on the platform under all three.
'Cache the shell, fetch the promise' and the requirements per page type; Core Web Vitals with their thresholds and dates, and the dated, caveated evidence that speed moves sales.
Technical SEO as part of the storefront's contract, and accessibility as a dated obligation (WCAG 2.2; the European Accessibility Act applying since 28 June 2025).
believe: A storefront renders facts it does not own; a new renderer moves rendering and glue, not facts.

can_do: Read field Core Web Vitals at the 75th percentile and trace a slow metric to its cause before choosing a remedy.

From Part I: the thirteen steps of an order, promise and handoff, the three status lines, 'system', 'the shop platform' for the hosted product and 'commerce platform' for the whole set of systems, business models and the four scale stages (Starting, Growing, Omnichannel, Group), the capability map, bounded context, system of record, single writer, events, idempotency and reconciliation.
Glosses already given: PSP, WMS, ERP, iPaaS, EDI, webhook, API call, SKU, channel, marketplace connector, 3PL, order hub and order management system, availability service, D2C, B2B, PIM, POS.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a headless proposal and field measurements, the reader decides from the measurements and the three needs, not from the promise of speed.
acceptance_criteria.probe: An agency proposes rebuilding a brand's three country storefronts as a headless application for about €240,000 and nine months, promising speed, flexible brand content and readiness for the future. Field measurements on mobile product pages at the 75th percentile show the main content in 2.1 seconds, interaction response in 310 milliseconds and layout shift of 0.08, and the slow interaction traces to scripts from eleven apps. Using only this chapter: should the brand accept, and what should it do instead?
acceptance_criteria.expected: No. Content loading and layout stability are already within Google's good thresholds (2.5 seconds, 0.1); interaction above 200 milliseconds is caused by app scripts, which a new renderer would not remove, so the remedy is a theme performance pass, an app-script audit and a performance budget. A content need is met by theme sections or a content system feeding the theme. Headless is for a shared front end across brands, a content-led site or a B2B portal the theme cannot express, with a team that can run a second production application; none applies to one brand with three storefront engineers.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The reader can say which parts of a product page are cached and which are fetched live, and what breaks when the rule is broken.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Using only this chapter: which parts of a product page can be cached and which must be fetched or checked live, and what goes wrong in each direction?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Product content, images, attributes and layout per market and language, category pages and editorial pages are cached, with request collapsing on a miss at peak; account prices, stock commitments, the cart and checkout are fetched or validated live, and public price or stock snapshots carry a freshness limit; account-specific answers are never shared across customers. A cached promise shows a wrong price or sells the last unit twice (the Price Drift, the Oversell); an uncacheable page saturates the renderer and the APIs behind it at peak.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The reader can say what the storefront owes search engines and shoppers with disabilities, and who owns it.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Using only this chapter: besides speed, what does a storefront owe search engines and shoppers with disabilities?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Product pages that can be crawled and indexed, whose rendered content and structured product data agree, with explicit rules for variants, filters, localized pages and retired products, checked by a named owner after each release; and WCAG 2.2 conformance of the theme and every app block, required for consumer e-commerce under the European Accessibility Act since 28 June 2025.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of the introduction alone (the callouts and the paragraphs before the first section heading) can predict the chapter's sections and the kind of evidence it uses.
acceptance_criteria.probe: After reading only the introduction: what will this chapter discuss, in what order, and with what kind of evidence?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Why a slow product page can lose a sale and why a new page that waits on the same slow price, stock or script inherits the problem; what a storefront and a headless storefront are, and what running one adds; Kestrel & Pine's three storefronts on one agency theme, its 41 apps and peak traffic 41 times an average hour, and Noor Visser's decision on the February 2027 headless proposal; Eva seeing the jacket's price, stock and delivery promise on her phone; following product pages to shoppers and search engines, comparing rendering models and judging when a separate storefront is worthwhile. Evidence: Kestrel & Pine's field measurements and dated vendor documentation and performance studies.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reverse outline of the draft, written without the spec, lists the same controlling ideas in the same order as sections[].paragraphs[].

thesis.question: How does the storefront reach the shopper's browser, and when does headless make sense?
thesis.claim: The storefront renders facts other systems own, from a platform-rendered theme or a headless front end on the vendor's runtime or elsewhere; checkout stays on the platform under every model. Content is cached per market at the edge; price, stock and cart are fetched or validated live. Headless pays only for a shared front end across brands, a content-led site or a B2B portal the theme cannot express, with a team to run it; never for speed alone.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that headless is the modern storefront: an agency-built front end on a fast framework makes pages faster and converts better, so a merchant with a slow theme should rebuild its storefront rather than fix what runs on the theme.
thesis.so_what: A merchant that accepts the claim reads field Core Web Vitals before any rebuild, traces a slow metric to its cause, sets a cache rule per page type, and asks a headless proposal which of the three needs it serves and who will run it in year two. In February 2027 Kestrel & Pine's agency proposed a headless rebuild on the platform vendor's edge runtime with a headless CMS (about €240,000 and nine months, plus a second runtime to operate; illustrative). Noor Visser measured the NL product pages on mobile at the 75th percentile (LCP 2.1 s, INP 310 ms, CLS 0.08), found the INP problem in eleven apps' scripts and declined. A quarter of agency time (about €38,000) went to a theme performance pass and an app-script audit, and by June 2027 INP measured 180 ms after six unused apps and four redundant scripts were removed. The decision is part of W4 and is revisited at the 2029 review.
thesis.how_why: The storefront owns templates, layout and scripts, not the catalog, prices, stock or cart, so a new renderer moves the rendering and the glue into the merchant's hands without moving any fact, and a slow price or stock answer or a heavy app script slows a headless page as much as a themed one. Content changes when the catalog changes, so it can be computed once and served to many shoppers from the edge, collapsing requests at peak; price, stock and cart change per shopper or per sale, and a cached copy of them is how the Price Drift and the Oversell reached the page. A headless front end is a second production application with on-call, caching rules, framework upgrades and API version pins, which a team of three that also runs the apps can carry only when the theme blocks a real need.

supporting_claims.claim: The storefront owns templates, layout, brand and browser scripts and renders facts other systems own (catalog, price, promotions, search, stock, delivery promise, cart, content), so a new renderer moves the rendering and the glue, not the facts.

The three rendering models (a theme rendered by the platform, headless on the vendor's runtime, headless anywhere) differ in who runs the renderer and where the templates live; checkout stays on the platform under all three.

Cache the shell, fetch the promise: content is cached per market and language and collapsed at peak, while account prices, stock commitments and the cart are fetched or validated live; public pages also serve search engines, so their rendered content, product data and URL rules must agree and have an owner.

Page experience is measured in the field at the 75th percentile and owed to every shopper; the evidence that speed moves sales is directional and dated, the usual cause of a slow page is the scripts rather than the rendering model, and accessibility is a dated obligation on the theme and every app block.

Headless pays only for a need the theme cannot meet (a shared front end across brands, a content-led site, a B2B portal) and a team that can run a second production application; never for speed alone, as Kestrel & Pine's measured decision shows.

role.contribution: Gives the part its surface to the shopper: the storefront as a renderer of facts it does not own, the three rendering models with checkout left on the platform, the rule 'cache the shell, fetch the promise' that the peak relies on, and the three needs that justify headless.

additional_patterns.applies_to: scene to in-practice: the agency's proposal, then Noor's answer

flow.rationale: The proposal and Noor's measurements come first so every later section answers part of them. What the storefront owns comes before the rendering models, because the models differ only in who renders facts the storefront does not own; the performance evidence follows the models directly, because it answers the agency's speed promise and the scene's measurements and shows that the rendering model is not the usual cause; accessibility sits beside it as the other requirement every page must meet; the cache rule follows, because it decides whether those requirements hold on a peak day, and technical SEO after it, because search engines read the same cached public pages; the evidence, accessibility, cache and SEO before the options, because the options are judged against them, including whether the theme and its app blocks can meet the accessibility obligation; the options before the stage table and Noor's decision, which apply them; the failures after the decision, in the book's fixed order. Putting the options before the cache rule and the evidence would ask the reader to judge headless before knowing what it would and would not change.

sections.heading: Three Rendering Models
sections.controlling_idea: Today's storefronts render on the server, so the three models differ in who runs the renderer and where the templates live: a theme rendered by the platform, headless on the vendor's runtime, or headless anywhere; checkout stays on the platform under all three.

advances_thesis.how: Sets out the three models with dated vendor examples and the checkout boundary.

flow.rationale: The rendering terms first, because the models are compared in them; then the models from the most platform-run to the most merchant-run, each with its dated examples, so each step adds one thing the merchant must run.

transition_in.carries_over: Headless moves the rendering and the glue.
transition_in.introduces: The ways the rendering can be organized.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Server-side rendering builds the full page on a server and client-side rendering builds it in the browser; early headless storefronts were slow client-rendered applications, but today's frameworks render on the server, so the models now differ in who runs the renderer and where the templates live.

In the first model a theme, a set of templates the platform's renderer turns into pages (Shopify's Liquid, BigCommerce's Stencil, Salesforce's SFRA), leaves rendering, caching, delivery, security and scale to the platform and the templates to the merchant.

evidence.what: Shopify Liquid themes; BigCommerce Stencil, 'BigCommerce's Handlebars-based theme engine'; Salesforce SFRA templates.
evidence.shows: Dated examples of the platform-rendered model.

transition_in.introduces: Model 1, the theme rendered by the platform.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Shopify's 2020 account of a dedicated Liquid renderer with several cache layers, four to six times faster than its predecessor and deployed regionally by 2022, is a dated example of the delivery infrastructure a theme inherits, not a measurement of today's service.

evidence.what: Storefront Renderer: database replicas, query cache, in-memory cache, full-page cache; 4x-6x faster (August 2020); regional deployment without the monolith (January 2022).
evidence.shows: What the platform runs on the merchant's behalf under model 1.

transition_in.carries_over: The platform runs rendering and caching.
transition_in.introduces: Shopify's dated account of that renderer.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The merchant inherits the delivery infrastructure but is limited by the platform's page types, which Shopify's Online Store 2.0 (29 June 2021) extended with JSON templates, sections and app blocks so templates need less direct editing.

evidence.what: Online Store 2.0, 29 June 2021: JSON templates, sections, app blocks.
evidence.shows: Shows the limit of model 1 and how the vendor loosened it.

transition_in.introduces: What it is limited by.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: In the second model the vendor supplies a storefront API and hosting and the merchant builds the front end, as with Shopify's Hydrogen and Oxygen, Salesforce's PWA Kit on Managed Runtime and Adobe Commerce as a Cloud Service on Edge Delivery Services.

evidence.what: Hydrogen with Storefront and Customer Account API clients, React Router 7 starter, Oxygen hosting (docs 2026-10); Oxygen on main plans at no extra cost (February 2023); PWA Kit on Managed Runtime; Adobe Commerce as a Cloud Service on Edge Delivery Services (20 October 2026).
evidence.shows: Dated examples of the vendor-runtime model.

transition_in.introduces: Model 2, headless on the vendor's runtime.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Checkout stays on the commerce platform under the vendor-runtime model: Hydrogen excludes checkout UI, and the merchant's application builds the cart and hands the shopper over.

sections.heading: Performance: What the Evidence Says, With Dates
sections.controlling_idea: Core Web Vitals measure real visitors at the 75th percentile against dated thresholds; the evidence that speed moves money is consistent in direction and weak in precision, and the usual culprit is scripts, not the rendering model.

advances_thesis.how: Gives the metrics, the dated evidence and its caveats, and the scripts as the usual cause.

flow.rationale: The metrics and their dated definitions first, close to the scene's measurements, which used them in one clause; then Google's ranking wording; then the business evidence with its caveats; then the reading that follows from it, applied back to the scene. The reading needs the evidence before it.

transition_in.introduces: How a page's speed is measured whichever model renders it, answering the agency's first promise.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Core Web Vitals are Google's three field metrics, assessed at the 75th percentile of page loads, mobile and desktop separately: LCP (good at 2.5 seconds or less), INP (200 milliseconds or less) and CLS (0.1 or less).

evidence.what: web.dev Web Vitals, updated 31 October 2024.
evidence.shows: Dates the metrics and thresholds the scene's numbers are read against.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: INP replaced first input delay on 12 March 2024, and Google's Search documentation 'highly recommend[s]' good Core Web Vitals and says they align with what its ranking systems reward, without stating a weight.

evidence.what: 'highly recommend[s]' good Core Web Vitals 'for success with Search'; they 'align with what our core ranking systems seek to reward'.
evidence.shows: Shows what Google says about ranking, and what it does not.
evidence.source: Google Search Central, accessed November 2026; web.dev INP blog, 2024

transition_in.introduces: Their date of change and their place in search ranking.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The evidence that speed moves money is consistent in direction and weak in precision: a six-year-old commissioned correlation study, self-selected case studies, and a vendor's own rules limiting what apps may cost.

evidence.what: Deloitte Ireland for Google (24 March 2020): 0.1 s faster went with +8.4% retail conversions and +9.2% average order value; commissioned, sites undisclosed, correlation.
evidence.shows: Direction with caveats.

evidence.what: web.dev cases: Vodafone Italy LCP 31% better, sales +8%; Lazada LCP 3x, mobile conversion +16.9%; Cdiscount +6% revenue in a Black Friday sale; self-selected.
evidence.shows: Direction without separation from redesigns.

evidence.what: Shopify: performance 'directly influences conversion rates...'; Theme Store minimum Lighthouse 60; apps 'shouldn't reduce Lighthouse performance scores by more than 10 points'; theme code and apps 'can slow down your site'.
evidence.shows: The vendor's own rules point at apps.
evidence.source: shopify.dev and Shopify Help Center, accessed November 2026

transition_in.introduces: What the evidence says about sales.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Faster is better, nobody can say by how much, and the usual culprit is the scripts rather than the rendering model: the vendor's ten-point cap on apps admits it, and Kestrel & Pine's INP of 310 milliseconds came from eleven apps' scripts.

evidence.what: Figure 3: Kestrel & Pine's INP of 310 ms was eleven apps' scripts, not the rendering model; good is 200 ms or less.
evidence.shows: Ties the general reading to the case.

transition_in.introduces: What they add up to, applied to Kestrel & Pine.

sections.heading: Accessibility Is a Requirement, Not a Performance Option
sections.controlling_idea: An accessible storefront lets every shopper complete the purchase; WCAG 2.2 states the standard, the European Accessibility Act has made it an obligation for consumer e-commerce since 28 June 2025, and it applies to the theme and every app block together.

advances_thesis.how: Makes accessibility a dated obligation on the theme and every app block.

flow.rationale: What accessibility means, then the standard, then the law, then Kestrel & Pine's place under it, then what that requires of a theme with apps: each step narrows to the merchant's own work.

transition_in.introduces: Accessibility, a requirement speed does not satisfy.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: An accessible storefront lets people find products, understand choices and pay with the ways they use a device, and a fast page still fails a customer who cannot use a form or a payment control.
WCAG 2.2, the W3C's Web Content Accessibility Guidelines, is a Recommendation dated 12 December 2024 with three conformance levels and four principles.

evidence.what: W3C WCAG 2.2, 12 December 2024.
evidence.shows: Dates the standard a storefront is tested against.

transition_in.introduces: The standard that states it.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The European Accessibility Act applies to consumer e-commerce services provided after 28 June 2025, with microenterprises exempt.

evidence.what: Directive (EU) 2019/882: services 'provided to consumers after 28 June 2025'; 'e-commerce services' listed; microenterprises (under 10 people, up to €2 million turnover) exempt.
evidence.shows: Makes accessibility a dated legal obligation.

transition_in.introduces: The law that makes it an obligation for e-commerce.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Kestrel & Pine, with 310 employees and three consumer storefronts, has been in scope since June 2025, while its B2B portal is not a consumer service, and national enforcement belongs to the regulation chapter.

evidence.what: 310 employees; three consumer storefronts; B2B portal.
evidence.shows: Places the running case in and out of scope.

transition_in.introduces: Kestrel & Pine inside and outside it.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: An accessible theme can still contain an unusable app block, so accessibility criteria apply to the theme, the inserted components and their combined purchase flow.

transition_in.introduces: What being in scope requires: the whole purchase flow, theme and app blocks together.

sections.heading: Cache the Shell, Fetch the Promise
sections.controlling_idea: Content that is the same for many shoppers is cached per market and language; answers that are promises to this shopper are fetched or validated live; the rule sets each page type's requirements and decides peak-day survival.

advances_thesis.how: States the cache rule, its mechanisms and its requirements per page type.

flow.rationale: The split first (what can be computed once and what cannot), then each side, then the rule's name, then the mechanisms that implement it on the platform and the headless layer, then the peak-day feature, and last the requirements per page type that apply it.

transition_in.carries_over: The page requirements of speed and accessibility.
transition_in.introduces: The decision that lets a page meet them on a peak day: which answers can be reused.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Some page content can be computed once and served repeatedly, while other answers depend on this shopper and this purchase.

Product content, images, attributes and layout per market and language, category pages, editorial pages and to a degree search facets are cacheable, because they change with the catalog or the campaign, not with each shopper.

transition_in.introduces: The first kind: what can be cached.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Account prices, stock commitments, the cart and checkout are validated live; public snapshots of price and availability need a freshness limit, account-specific answers are never shared, and stale answers are how the Price Drift and the Oversell reached the page.

evidence.what: The Price Drift and the Black Friday Oversell, seen from the page's side.
evidence.shows: Shows what a cached promise costs.

evidence.what: Figure 4: the cached shell served many times while price, stock badge and cart are fetched for this shopper.
evidence.shows: Pictures the split.

transition_in.introduces: What must be validated live.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: 'Cache the shell, fetch the promise' names the rule of serving cached content, refreshing changing facts and validating purchase terms, and Shopify's full-page cache supplies it at the platform level.

transition_in.carries_over: The two sides of the split.
transition_in.introduces: The rule's name and its platform mechanism.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: At the headless layer the same idea appears as incremental static regeneration, which Vercel documents as serving the cached page while regenerating it, with e-commerce catalogs as the first use case, request collapsing per region and stale content served if regeneration fails.

evidence.what: Vercel ISR documentation (updated 28 August 2026): catalogs 'that need current pricing and availability without rebuilding the entire site'; concurrent requests collapsed 'into one function invocation per region, protecting your backend during traffic spikes'.
evidence.shows: The headless layer implements the same rule.

transition_in.introduces: The same rule at the headless layer.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Request collapsing is the peak-day feature: when 41 times the normal traffic hits one hero product, the backend sees one request instead of thousands; on the 2026 peak night Kestrel & Pine's cached pages held while the stock sync chain behind the stock badge did not.

evidence.what: Figure 5: Eva's product page arrives from the edge cache first; the storefront then fetches availability and price.
evidence.shows: Shows the sequence on the running case.

transition_in.carries_over: Request collapsing among the documented features.
transition_in.introduces: Why it matters on the peak day.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Each page type gets its own freshness, consistency, speed and peak-day requirement under the rule, from fully cached product content to a live, platform-owned cart and checkout.

evidence.what: Requirements per page type: product and category content, price shown, stock badge and delivery promise, search results, logged-in B2B pages, cart and checkout, against how fresh, how consistent, how fast and on a peak day.
evidence.shows: Turns the rule into a requirement a team can set per page.

transition_in.carries_over: The rule and its peak-day feature.
transition_in.introduces: The rule applied to each page type.

sections.heading: Technical SEO and Product Discoverability
sections.controlling_idea: Public product pages must also be discoverable by search engines: crawlable links and sitemaps, product content and structured data in the initial HTML that agree with the live facts, an explicit policy per kind of URL, distinct crawl and index controls, and a named owner who checks them after each release.

advances_thesis.how: Extends the cache rule to search engines and gives the public pages' discoverability an owner.

flow.rationale: Definitions first; then a path to every product, then what an engine reads on the page, then the policy for each kind of URL, then the controls that block crawling or indexing, then who owns and checks it all: each step assumes the one before.

transition_in.carries_over: Cached public pages and their freshness limits.
transition_in.introduces: The second reader of those public pages: search engines.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A fast product page can still be hard to find: search-engine optimization rests on letting engines crawl and index pages, and the platform controls much of that foundation through links, rendered content, URLs and product data.
Every product to be found needs a path of ordinary HTML links, supported by a sitemap, because Google generally does not search a store's own search box.

evidence.what: Google Search Central, ecommerce navigation guidance (accessed 9 November 2026).
evidence.shows: Supports links and sitemaps as the path to discovery.

transition_in.introduces: The first requirement: a path to every product.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Google can execute JavaScript but renders in a separate step and other crawlers may not, so useful product content and a descriptive title belong in the initial HTML; server rendering or pre-rendering supports this, and headless alone gives no SEO advantage.

evidence.what: Google's JavaScript SEO guidance.
evidence.shows: Supports server rendering or pre-rendering for discoverable content.

transition_in.introduces: What the engine finds when it arrives: the rendered page.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Structured data names the product's facts for machines, Google recommends it in the initial HTML, and it should come from the same records as the visible page and the product feed.

evidence.what: Google's merchant listing guidance: product markup in the initial HTML.
evidence.shows: Supports generating markup with the page.

transition_in.carries_over: Product content in the initial HTML.
transition_in.introduces: The product facts named for machines.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The cache rule serves search engines too: public price and availability snapshots need a maximum age and coordinated updates in HTML, markup and feeds, so machines do not read yesterday's price, and good markup makes a page eligible for richer results without guaranteeing them.

transition_in.carries_over: Structured data from the same records.
transition_in.introduces: The cache rule applied to what machines read.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Variants, filters and translations multiply the URLs a platform can publish, so each kind of page needs an explicit policy for its address before crawlers see it.

evidence.what: Policy per case: product variants (canonical URL), filters and sorting (index chosen landing pages, limit crawling), languages and countries (hreflang), temporary stockouts (keep the page), moves and retirement (301/308, 404/410).
evidence.shows: Gives each kind of URL a decision and its reason.

transition_in.carries_over: Pages that agree with the live facts.
transition_in.introduces: The addresses those pages are published under.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: These policies follow Google's guidance on ecommerce URLs, faceted navigation, localized versions and site moves, checked 9 November 2026, and the stockout row is an implementation recommendation, because a sell-out and a retirement are different events.

evidence.what: Google Search Central and Google Crawling Infrastructure pages on ecommerce URLs, faceted navigation, localized versions and site moves, accessed 9 November 2026.
evidence.shows: Dates and sources the table; labels the author's own row.

transition_in.introduces: Its sources and the one row that is the author's recommendation.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: robots.txt controls fetching and noindex controls inclusion in results; blocking crawling can hide a noindex, neither protects private data, and a release must not carry test-site exclusions onto public product pages.

evidence.what: Google's guidance on blocking indexing with noindex.
evidence.shows: Supports the distinction between the two controls.

transition_in.carries_over: Policies that decide which pages should be found.
transition_in.introduces: The two controls that keep pages out, and how they differ.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The storefront team should own these rules with catalog and marketing choosing the landing pages, check one jacket's localized pages and variants through a price change and a stockout, inspect and monitor with Search Console after template changes, and preserve the URL policy during migration.

transition_in.carries_over: The links, rendering, markup, URL policies and controls.
transition_in.introduces: Who owns them and how they are checked.

sections.heading: The Choices and Their Trade-Offs
sections.controlling_idea: A merchant on a hosted platform has four options (the disciplined theme, the theme plus a CMS, headless on the vendor's runtime, headless anywhere), and headless is chosen only when the theme cannot express a shared design across brands, a content-led site or a B2B portal, and a team can own on-call, caching, upgrades and API versions.

advances_thesis.how: States the decision rule against the four options.

flow.rationale: The four options and their trade-offs, then the rule for choosing among them, then mobile apps, the other front end proposed in speed's name, judged by the same rule.

transition_in.carries_over: Speed, accessibility, caching and discoverability, all of which can be met on a theme.
transition_in.introduces: The other needs a choice of rendering model rests on, and the options.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The realistic options for a merchant on a hosted platform are four, from the disciplined theme to headless anywhere, and they differ in who runs rendering and caching, flexibility, peak-day posture, the team needed and when each is right.

evidence.what: Four options against who runs rendering and caching, flexibility, peak-day posture, team needed and when right.
evidence.shows: Sets the options side by side so the team cost is visible.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Headless is right only when the theme cannot express a shared design across brands, an editorially driven site or a B2B portal's account pricing and approvals, and when a team will own on-call, caching, framework upgrades and API versions after the agency leaves; speed alone establishes neither.

transition_in.introduces: The rule for choosing between them.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A progressive web app is mostly the headless question in disguise, since a server-rendered storefront can be made installable, while a native app is a second storefront that must show the same prices, stock and promises and is justified by loyalty, push and in-store features, not speed.

evidence.what: web.dev: a PWA is a website 'built and enhanced with modern APIs' that can be installed, work offline and send push notifications.
evidence.shows: Defines the term before the comparison.

transition_in.carries_over: The rule for choosing a front end.
transition_in.introduces: Mobile apps, the other front end proposed in speed's name.

sections.heading: Across Scale Stages: When It Fits and When It Limits
sections.controlling_idea: The disciplined theme fits from Starting through Omnichannel; at Group scale a shared front end becomes valuable, and Omnichannel scale alone is no reason to build one.

advances_thesis.how: Applies the rule to each scale stage.

transition_in.introduces: The rule applied stage by stage.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The theme is kept while it meets the requirements; Group scale makes a shared front end more valuable, and Omnichannel scale alone does not justify one.

evidence.what: Four stages with what is typical, what becomes necessary and warning signs of outgrowing the approach, Kestrel & Pine at Omnichannel.
evidence.shows: Signs a merchant can check against its own storefront and proposals.

Putting the checks first placed replacement advice before a decision not to replace, which both round-2 readers found unclear.

sections.heading: When It Goes Wrong
sections.controlling_idea: Storefronts fail as cached promises, uncacheable peaks, script sprawl, forked themes, drifting headless front ends, bots at the front door and inaccessible flows, each with a sign to detect and a recovery.

advances_thesis.how: Shows the chapter's rules as recoveries from named failures.

transition_in.introduces: The ways a storefront decision goes wrong, mapped to the chapter's named failure patterns.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Seven storefront failures recur, from a cached promise to an inaccessible checkout, and each has a sign to detect and a recovery drawn from the chapter's rules.

evidence.what: Seven failures: a cached promise, the uncacheable peak, script sprawl, the forked theme, the headless storefront that drifted, bots at the front door, an inaccessible storefront; what each looks like, detection and recovery.
evidence.shows: Turns each rule into a detection and a recovery.

evidence.what: Commerce.com (formerly BigCommerce) Q2 2026 filing reported lower gross margin; an earnings-call summary attributed part of it to hosting costs from AI crawlers and agents (6 August 2026).
evidence.shows: Dated evidence for the bot row, labelled as a secondary attribution.

conclusion.heading: What to Take Away
conclusion.synthesis: The slow product page at the start has one answer across the chapter: the storefront owns templates and scripts, not facts, so its speed is found by measuring the page in the field and tracing the slow metric, which at Kestrel & Pine led to eleven apps' scripts, not to the renderer. The same split governs the rest: what is the same for many shoppers is cached and shown to search engines, what is a promise is fetched or validated live, and the renderer changes only for a need the theme cannot meet with a team to run it.
conclusion.so_what: A merchant can answer a headless proposal by reading field Core Web Vitals, tracing the slow metric, setting a cache rule per page type and asking which of the three needs the proposal serves and who runs it in year two; Kestrel & Pine spent about €38,000 on a theme performance pass instead of €240,000 on a rebuild.

callback.to: The opening's slow product page whose delay may come from a price service, a stock lookup or an app script.
callback.how: p54 names where Kestrel & Pine's delay came from and why a new page would have inherited it.

takeaway.content: Measure product and category pages in the field at the 75th percentile on mobile, trace any slow metric to its cause, budget app scripts, set what is cached and what is fetched per page type, give public-page discoverability and accessibility an owner, and consider headless only for a shared front end, a content-led site or a B2B portal the theme cannot express, with a team that can run it.
